questions.q: What is the immediate emotional state of Matilda during the ball, and which two textual phrases best capture it?
questions.a: Matilda feels ecstatic triumph — "drunk with pleasure" and "floating on a cloud of happiness" capture her artificial euphoria. A wrong answer like "she feels grateful" or "she feels anxious" reveals the student misses that this is pure, unselfconscious vanity fulfilled — the text explicitly says she forgot her husband, her poverty, everything except her own success.

questions.q: Why does Maupassant spend nearly a page describing Matilda's success at the ball when the story is really about the necklace loss?
questions.a: The extended description creates dramatic irony — the reader sees the height of her fake glory, making the inevitable fall more devastating. A wrong answer like "to show she was happy" or "to describe the party" reveals the student doesn't understand structural contrast: the ball's length mirrors how completely the necklace consumes her identity — she becomes the necklace.

questions.q: In the ball scene, Matilda's husband Loisel falls asleep in a side room. Apply the concept of "foil character" to explain what Loisel's sleep reveals about Matilda at this moment.
questions.a: Loisel's sleep highlights Matilda's total self-absorption — he waits hours while she dances, showing she no longer needs him now that she has the necklace's status. Steps: (1) Identify Loisel's action (sleeping in anteroom). (2) Note Matilda's reaction (she doesn't check on him, doesn't care). (3) Contrast: earlier she needed him for the invitation, dress, necklace — now she's independent. (4) Conclude: the necklace replaces her husband as her source of worth. A wrong answer like "Loisel is tired" misses the symbolic shift — the necklace has become her true partner.

questions.q: Analyze how Maupassant uses sensory imagery in the ball scene to make Matilda's triumph feel physically overwhelming, and why this matters for the story's irony.
questions.a: Maupassant uses kinetic ("danced madly"), thermal ("drunk with pleasure"), and spatial ("floating on a cloud") imagery to make the joy visceral — the reader feels the spin, the heat, the weightlessness. This matters because the body remembers the pleasure even after the mind knows it's fake; the sensory richness makes the later physical suffering (scrubbing floors, carrying water) a cruel bodily echo. A wrong answer listing images without connecting to irony shows the student can spot devices but not analyze their structural purpose.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "The ball is the only night Matilda is truly happy in the entire story." Defend or refute using textual evidence.
questions.a: Refute — the ball gives her *vanity satisfaction*, not happiness. Evidence: she "forgot her husband" and "thought of nothing but her triumph" — true happiness involves connection, not erasure of loved ones. Also, her joy is parasitic on a lie (the fake necklace). The ten years later, though miserable, contain dignity and shared struggle with Loisel — a deeper, realer bond. A wrong answer agreeing reveals the student confuses external validation with internal fulfillment, missing Maupassant's critique of materialism.

questions.q: Create a 4-line diary entry Matilda might write the morning after the ball, capturing her emotional state before discovering the loss. Use first person and include one sensory detail from the text.
questions.a: Example: "January 19 / Still spinning from last night — the violin's hum in my fingers, the Minister's wife asking my name. I existed. / No poverty, no clerk husband, just light on diamonds." Criteria: first person, one sensory detail (violin/hum/light), shows the fragile ego-construction. A poor entry like "Had fun at party. Necklace pretty." reveals the student cannot inhabit the character's psychological complexity — they reduce the climax to plot points.
